danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Når man ser et dyr dø, føler man rædsel: noget der ligner ens eget væsen, forgår for ens øjne. Men når det er et elsket og nært menneske, der dør, er der foruden denne rædsel over livets udslukning et brud, et åndeligt sår, der ligesom et fysisk sår sommetider er dødeligt og sommetider heler, men altid gør ondt og trækker sig sammen ved enhver ydre irritation.

Efter fyrst Andrej Bolkonskijs (fyrst Andrej) død følte Natasja og prinsesse Marja begge dette. Nedtrykte i ånden og med lukkede øjne for den truende sky af død, der svævede over dem, vovede de ikke at se livet i øjnene. De vogtede omhyggeligt deres åbne sår mod enhver grov og smertefuld berøring. Alt: en vogn der hastigt kørte forbi i gaden, en tilkaldelse til middag, stuepigen der spurgte, hvilken kjole der skulle lægges frem, eller endnu værre et ord af uoprigtig eller svag medfølelse, virkede som en fornærmelse, irriterede smertefuldt såret, afbrød den nødvendige stilhed, hvori de begge forsøgte at lytte til det strenge og forfærdelige kor, der stadig genlød i deres fantasi, og forhindrede dem i at skue ind i de mystiske, grænseløse vidder, som for et øjeblik havde åbnet sig for dem.
Kun når de var alene sammen, var de fri for sådanne krænkelser og smerter. De talte kun lidt, selv til hinanden, og når de gjorde det, var det om meget uvæsentlige ting.

Begge undgik enhver hentydning til fremtiden. At indrømme muligheden af en fremtid syntes dem at krænke hans minde. Endnu mere omhyggeligt undgik de alt, der vedrørte ham, der var død. Det forekom dem, at det, de havde gennemlevet og oplevet, ikke kunne udtrykkes i ord, og at enhver henvisning til detaljerne i hans liv krænkede den majestæt og hellighed, der omgav det mysterium, som var sket for deres øjne.

Den vedvarende afholdenhed fra tale og den stadige undvigelse af alt, der kunne føre hen til emnet — denne standsning på alle sider ved grænsen af det, de ikke måtte nævne — bragte med endnu større renhed og klarhed det for deres bevidsthed, som de begge følte.

Men ren og fuldstændig sorg er lige så umulig som ren og fuldstændig glæde. Prinsesse Marja, der som absolut og uafhængig herskerinde over sin egen skæbne og værge og opdrager for sin nevø var den første, der blev kaldt tilbage til livet fra det sorgens rige, hvor hun havde dvælet de første fjorten dage. Hun modtog breve fra sine slægtninge, som hun måtte besvare; det værelse, hvor lille Nikolaj var anbragt, var fugtigt, og han begyndte at hoste; Alpatytj kom til Jaroslavl med beretninger om forholdene på deres godser og med råd og forslag om, at de skulle vende tilbage til Moskva til huset på Vozdvizjenka-gaden, som var forblevet ubeskadiget og kun behøvede små reparationer. Livet stod ikke stille, og det var nødvendigt at leve. Hvor svært det end var for prinsesse Marja at træde ud af det ensomme livs kontemplation, hun hidtil havde levet i, og hvor ked af det og næsten flov hun følte sig ved at forlade Natasja alene, så krævede livets gøremål hendes opmærksomhed, og hun gav uvilkårligt efter for dem. Hun gennemgik regnskaberne med Alpatytj, rådførte sig med Dessalles om sin nevø og traf forberedelser til rejsen til Moskva.
Natasja blev alene, og fra det tidspunkt prinsesse Marja begyndte at forberede afrejsen, holdt hun sig også væk fra hende.

Prinsesse Marja bad grevinden om at lade Natasja rejse med til Moskva, og begge forældre tog glad imod tilbuddet, for de så, at deres datter tabte kræfterne dag for dag, og mente, at et sceneskifte og Moskva-lægernes råd ville gøre hende godt.

»Jeg rejser ingen steder hen,« svarede Natasja, da dette blev foreslået hende. »Vær venlig bare at lade mig være!« Og hun løb ud af værelset, mens hun med nød og næppe holdt tårer af vrede og irritation snarere end af sorg tilbage.

Da hun følte sig forladt af prinsesse Marja og alene med sin sorg, tilbragte Natasja det meste af tiden i sit værelse alene, sammenkrøbet med ben og det hele i sofaens hjørne, mens hun knitrede og vred noget med sine slanke, nervøse fingre og stirrede stift og ubevægeligt på det, hendes blik tilfældigvis faldt på. Denne ensomhed udmattede og plagede hende, men hun havde absolut brug for den. Så snart nogen trådte ind, rejste hun sig hurtigt, skiftede stilling og ansigtsudtryk og greb en bog eller noget håndarbejde, tilsyneladende utålmodigt ventende på, at den ubudne gæst skulle gå.
Hun følte hele tiden, at hun hvert øjeblik kunne trænge igennem til det, som — med en forfærdelig spørgen, der var for stor for hendes kræfter — hendes åndelige blik var rettet mod.

En dag hen imod slutningen af december sad Natasja, bleg og mager, klædt i en sort uldkjole med sit flettede hår skødesløst slået op i en knude, sammenkrøbet med ben og det hele i sofaens hjørne, mens hun nervøst krøllede og glattede enden af sit bælte og kiggede på et hjørne af døren.

Hun stirrede i den retning, han var gået — til den anden side af livet. Og den anden side af livet, som hun aldrig før havde tænkt på, og som tidligere havde forekommet hende så fjern og usandsynlig, var nu nærmere og mere beslægtet og mere forståelig end denne side af livet, hvor alt var enten tomhed og ødemark eller lidelse og vanære.

Hun stirrede derhen, hvor hun vidste, han var; men hun kunne ikke forestille sig ham anderledes, end han havde været her. Hun så ham nu igen, som han havde været i Mytisjtji, i Troitsa og i Jaroslavl.
Hun så hans ansigt, hørte hans stemme, gentog hans ord og sine egne, og udtænkte sommetider andre ord, de kunne have sagt.

Dér ligger han tilbagelænet i en lænestol i sin fløjlskappe, med hovedet hvilende på sin tynde, blege hånd. Hans bryst er frygteligt indsunket og hans skuldre løftet. Hans læber er fast lukkede, hans øjne glimt, og en rynke kommer og går på hans blege pande. Det ene ben sitrer næppe mærkeligt, men hurtigt. Natasja ved, at han kæmper med en forfærdelig smerte. »Hvordan er den smerte? Hvorfor har han den smerte? Hvad føler han? Hvordan gør det ondt?« tænkte Natasja. Han bemærkede, at hun betragtede ham, løftede øjnene og begyndte at tale alvorligt:

»Én ting ville være forfærdelig,« sagde han, »at binde sig for evigt til et lidende menneske. Det ville være en evig pine.« Og han så spørgende på hende. Natasja svarede som sædvanlig, inden hun nåede at tænke over, hvad hun ville sige. Hun sagde: »Det her kan ikke blive ved — det holder ikke. Du bliver rask — helt rask.«

Hun så ham nu forfra i den scene og genoplevede, hvad hun dengang havde følt. Hun huskede hans lange, triste og strenge blik ved de ord og forstod den bebrejdelse og fortvivlelse, der lå i det langvarige blik.

»Jeg sagde ja,« sagde Natasja nu til sig selv, »ja, at det ville være forfærdeligt, hvis han altid fortsatte med at lide. Dengang sagde jeg det kun, fordi det ville have været forfærdeligt for ham, men han forstod det anderledes. Han troede, det ville være forfærdeligt for mig. Han ønskede dengang stadig at leve og frygtede døden. Og jeg sagde det så kejtet og dumt! Jeg sagde ikke, hvad jeg mente. Jeg tænkte noget helt andet. Havde jeg sagt, hvad jeg tænkte, ville jeg have sagt: selv om han skulle blive ved med at dø, dø hele tiden for mine øjne, ville jeg have været lykkelig sammenlignet med det, jeg er nu. Nu er der intet... ingen. Vidste han det? Nej, han vidste det ikke og vil aldrig vide det. Og nu kan det aldrig, aldrig gøres godt igen.« Og nu syntes han igen at sige de samme ord til hende, men i hendes fantasi gav Natasja ham denne gang et andet svar. Hun standsede ham og sagde: »Forfærdeligt for dig, men ikke for mig! Du ved, at der for mig ikke er noget i livet uden dig, og at lide med dig er den største lykke for mig,« og han tog hendes hånd og trykkede den, som han havde trykket den den forfærdelige aften fire dage før sin død. Og i sin fantasi sagde hun andre ømme og kærlige ord, som hun kunne have sagt dengang, men kun sagde nu: »Jeg elsker dig!... dig! Elsker, elsker...« sagde hun, pressede krampagtigt sine hænder sammen og bed tænderne sammen i en fortvivlet anstrengelse...

Hun blev overvældet af sød sorg, og tårerne steg allerede i hendes øjne; da spurgte hun pludselig sig selv, hvem hun sagde dette til. Alt hylledes igen i hård, tør forvirring, og igen stirrede hun med anstrengt rynket pande mod den verden, hvor han var. Og nu, nu syntes det, at hun trængte ind i mysteriet... Men i det øjeblik, da det ufattelige syntes at åbenbare sig for hende, slog en høj raslen af dørhåndtaget smertefuldt ind i hendes ører. Duniasja, hendes stuepige, trådte hurtigt og brat ind i værelset med et forskrækket udtryk i ansigtet og uden at vise hensyn til sin herskerinde.
»Kom straks til Deres papa, vær så venlig!« sagde hun med et mærkeligt, ophidset udtryk. »En ulykke... om Pjotr Iljitj (Petja)... et brev,« sluttede hun med et hulk.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: When we see a dying animal, we feel a sense of horror: something made of the same substance as ourselves is perishing before our eyes. But when it is a beloved and intimate person who is dying, besides this horror at the extinguishing of life, there is a tearing apart, a spiritual wound that, like a physical wound, is sometimes fatal and sometimes heals, but always aches and flinches at any rough, irritating touch.

After Prince Andrew's death, Natasha and Princess Mary both felt this. Crushed in spirit and closing their eyes before the menacing cloud of death that hung over them, they dared not look life in the face. They carefully guarded their raw wounds from any harsh or painful contact. Everything—a carriage rattling quickly past in the street, a summons to dinner, the maid's question about what dress to prepare, or worst of all, any word of insincere or halfhearted sympathy—felt like an insult, painfully irritating the wound, interrupting the necessary silence in which they both tried to listen to the solemn and terrible chorus still echoing in their minds, and preventing them from gazing into those mysterious, infinite vistas that had for an instant opened before them.
Only when they were alone together were they free from such assaults. They spoke little even to each other, and when they did, it was about trivial things.

Both avoided any mention of the future. To acknowledge the possibility of a future seemed to them an insult to his memory. Even more carefully did they avoid anything connected with him who was dead. It seemed that what they had lived through and experienced could not be expressed in words, and that any reference to the details of his life would violate the majesty and sacredness of the mystery that had been accomplished before their eyes.

The constant restraint from speaking, the careful avoidance of everything that might lead to the forbidden subject—this halting on all sides at the boundary of what they could not mention—brought before their minds with even greater purity and clarity what they were both feeling.

But pure and complete grief is as impossible as pure and complete joy. Princess Mary, in her role as the sole and independent guardian of her own fate and of her nephew's upbringing, was the first to be called back to life from that realm of sorrow in which she had lived for the first two weeks. She received letters from relatives that required replies; the room where little Nicholas had been placed was damp and he began to cough; Alpatych came to Yaroslavl with reports on their affairs and suggestions that they return to Moscow, to the house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived intact and needed only minor repairs. Life would not stand still, and it was necessary to go on living. Hard as it was for Princess Mary to emerge from her secluded world of contemplation, and sorry and almost ashamed as she felt to leave Natasha alone, the demands of daily life required her attention and she involuntarily yielded to them. She went through the accounts with Alpatych, consulted with Dessalles about her nephew, and gave orders and made preparations for the journey to Moscow.
Natasha was left alone and, from the time Princess Mary began preparing for departure, withdrew from her too.

Princess Mary asked the countess to let Natasha travel with her to Moscow, and both parents gladly accepted the offer, seeing their daughter losing strength every day and believing that a change of scene and Moscow doctors would do her good.
"I'm not going anywhere," Natasha replied when this was proposed. "Please just leave me alone!" And she ran out of the room, barely holding back tears of irritation and vexation rather than sorrow.

After feeling herself abandoned by Princess Mary and left alone in her grief, Natasha spent most of her time in her room by herself, sitting huddled up with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, tearing and twisting something with her slender, nervous fingers, staring intently at whatever her eyes happened to fall on. This solitude exhausted and tormented her, but she desperately needed it. The moment anyone came in, she would jump up quickly, change her position and expression, and pick up a book or some sewing, clearly waiting impatiently for the intruder to leave.
She felt as though at any moment she might break through to that thing on which—with a terrible questioning too great for her strength—her whole being was fixed.

One day toward the end of December, Natasha, pale and thin, dressed in a black woolen gown with her braided hair carelessly twisted into a knot, sat crouched with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, nervously crumpling and smoothing the end of her sash while staring at a corner of the door.

She was gazing in the direction he had gone—to the other side of life. And that other side of life, which she had never thought about before and which had always seemed so distant and improbable, was now nearer and more familiar and more real to her than this side, where everything was either emptiness and desolation or suffering and humiliation.
She was gazing toward where she knew him to be; but she could not picture him other than as he had been here. She saw him again as he had been at Mytishchi, at Troitsa, and at Yaroslavl.
She saw his face, heard his voice, repeated his words and her own, and sometimes invented other words they might have said.

There he is, lying back in an armchair in his velvet cloak, leaning his head on his thin, pale hand. His chest is terribly hollow and his shoulders raised. His lips are pressed firmly together, his eyes glitter, and a wrinkle comes and goes on his pale forehead. One of his legs twitches just perceptibly, but rapidly. Natasha knows he is struggling with terrible pain. "What is that pain like? Why does he have it? What does he feel? How does it hurt him?" she thought. He noticed her watching him, raised his eyes, and began to speak seriously:

"One thing would be terrible," he said, "to bind oneself forever to a suffering man. It would be continual torture." And he looked at her searchingly. Natasha, as usual, answered before she had time to think. She said: "This can't go on—it won't. You will get well—completely well."

She now replayed that scene from the beginning and relived what she had felt then. She recalled his long, sad, and severe look at those words and understood the meaning of the reproach and despair in that prolonged gaze.

"I agreed," Natasha now said to herself, "that it would be terrible if he always continued to suffer. I said it then only because it would have been terrible for him. But he understood it differently. He thought it would be terrible for me. He still wanted to live then, and he feared death. And I said it so clumsily and stupidly! I didn't say what I meant. I thought something entirely different. If I had said what I was actually thinking, I would have said: even if he had to go on dying, dying continually before my eyes, I would have been happy compared to what I am now. Now there is nothing... nobody. Did he know that? No. He didn't know and never will. And now it can never, never be put right." And now he seemed to be saying the same words to her again, but this time, in her imagination, Natasha gave him a different answer. She stopped him and said: "Terrible for you, but not for me! You know that there is nothing in life for me but you, and to suffer with you is the greatest happiness I could have." And he took her hand and pressed it as he had pressed it on that terrible evening four days before his death. And in her imagination she said other tender and loving words that she might have said then but only spoke now: "I love you!... You!... I love, love..." she whispered, clenching her hands together and gritting her teeth with desperate effort...

She was overcome by sweet sorrow and tears were already rising in her eyes; then suddenly she asked herself to whom she was saying this. Again everything was shrouded in hard, dry confusion, and again with a strained frown she peered toward the world where he was. And now—now it seemed she was about to penetrate the mystery... But at the instant when the incomprehensible seemed about to reveal itself, a loud rattle of the door handle struck painfully on her ears. Dunyasha, her maid, burst into the room quickly and abruptly, with a frightened look and no concern for her mistress.
"Come to your father at once, please!" she said with a strange, agitated look. "A misfortune... about Pyotr Ilyich... a letter," she finished with a sob.
